Treat filters, search, sorting and pagination as one public query contract

Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination

Architecture milestone

Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract.

A collection endpoint is a query interface
GET /tasks is not just an array-returning function. It is a public query interface between clients and a dataset. A
professional contract needs explicit choices about scope, filters, search, order, pagination, defaults, limits, and
response metadata.

Concern                          Question

Scope                            Which Tasks may this endpoint expose?

Filter                           Which exact attributes narrow the collection?

Search                           Which text fields participate and with what semantics?

Sort                             Which fields may control ordering?

Stability                        How are ties broken?

Pagination                       How many rows may one request return?

Metadata                         How will a UI know whether more pages exist?

Query parameters express collection state
Collection choices normally belong in the URL because they describe which representation of the collection the client
wants. This makes URLs bookmarkable, shareable, inspectable in DevTools, and repeatable during debugging.

/tasks?status=IN_PROGRESS&priority=HIGH&page=2&pageSize=20

Avoid endpoint explosion
Do not create one route for every filter combination such as /high-priority-tasks, /completed-tasks,
/my-high-priority-tasks. Keep the resource stable and express queryable collection state with validated parameters.

Weak design                                                   Stronger collection design

/tasks/high-priority                                          /tasks?priority=HIGH

/tasks/completed                                              /tasks?status=DONE

/searchTasks?q=x                                              /tasks?search=x

/tasks/page/2                                                 /tasks?page=2

Later authorization will narrow scope further

A query parameter can ask for projectId or assigneeId, but it must never be trusted as proof that the caller is allowed to see
that scope. Authorization arrives later and will intersect with these filters.

Query DTOs & Zod Validation
Normalize strings, coerce numbers, apply defaults, cap page size, and reject unsupported
parameters

Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Raw query strings

v

Zod validation

v

TaskListQueryDto

v

TasksService

Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract.

Validate query strings at the HTTP boundary
Query strings arrive as strings. page=2 is initially the string "2", not the number 2. Phase 15 uses Zod coercion for
numeric pagination fields and strict allow-lists for enums and sort options.

import { z } from "zod";
import {
TaskPriority,
TaskStatus,
} from "../generated/prisma/client";

export const taskSortFieldSchema = z.enum([
"createdAt",
"updatedAt",
"dueAt",
"title",
]);

export const sortOrderSchema = z.enum(["asc", "desc"]);

export const taskListQuerySchema = z.strictObject({
projectId: z.uuid().optional(),
assigneeId: z.uuid().optional(),
status: z.enum(TaskStatus).optional(),
priority: z.enum(TaskPriority).optional(),
search: z.string().trim().min(1).max(100).optional(),
sort: taskSortFieldSchema.default("createdAt"),
order: sortOrderSchema.default("desc"),
page: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).default(1),
pageSize: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(100).default(20),
});

export type TaskListQueryDto = z.infer<typeof taskListQuerySchema>;
export type TaskSortField = z.infer<typeof taskSortFieldSchema>;
export type SortOrder = z.infer<typeof sortOrderSchema>;

Why defaults belong in the boundary schema
Defaults such as page=1, pageSize=20, sort=createdAt, and order=desc are part of the API contract. Applying them
once at validation means TasksService receives a normalized query instead of repeatedly handling undefined values.

Request                                                   Validated meaning

/tasks                                                    page=1, pageSize=20, createdAt desc

?page=0                                                   400 - page must be >= 1

?pageSize=1000                                            400 - server cap is 100

?sort=dropTable                                           400 - field is not allow-listed

?status=almost_done                                       400 - invalid enum value

?search=                                                  400 after trim/min length

Integrate with NestJS 12
@Get()
findAll(
@Query(new StandardSchemaValidationPipe(taskListQuerySchema))
query: TaskListQueryDto,
) {
return this.tasksService.findAll(query);
}

Boundary rule

Do not pass raw query strings into Prisma. Normalize and constrain them first. This is both safer and easier to reason about.

Why pageSize has a hard maximum
Without a server-controlled cap, a client can request pageSize=1000000 and effectively bypass pagination. The
product may later choose 50 or 200, but the backend must own the upper bound.

Prisma Filtering & where Design
Translate only approved public filters into Prisma query objects

Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Validated filters

v

Prisma where

v

SQL predicates

Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract.

Build Prisma where from validated filters
After validation, each optional filter can be translated into a Prisma TaskWhereInput. The service should build this
intentionally instead of forwarding the entire query object to Prisma.

private buildWhere(query: TaskListQueryDto): Prisma.TaskWhereInput {
return {
...(query.projectId ? { projectId: query.projectId } : {}),
...(query.assigneeId ? { assigneeId: query.assigneeId } : {}),
...(query.status ? { status: query.status } : {}),
...(query.priority ? { priority: query.priority } : {}),
};
}

Figure 1 - Filter translation

URL query string

v

Zod normalizes values

v

TaskListQueryDto

v

buildWhere()

v

Prisma TaskWhereInput

v

PostgreSQL WHERE predicates

The transport contract is translated into persistence-specific query input inside the service layer.

AND is the natural default
The example means projectId + status + priority filters all apply together. That is usually what users expect when they
add several table filters: narrow the result set by all selected criteria.

Relation filters remain possible
Prisma supports relation filters, but do not expose every relational capability as a public query parameter. Add only
filters the product genuinely needs, document them, validate them, then index the resulting workload if measurements
justify it.

Query DTO is not Prisma input

TaskListQueryDto is our public HTTP contract. Prisma.TaskWhereInput is an internal persistence shape. Keeping the
translation explicit prevents clients from gaining accidental access to arbitrary database query capability.

Search Semantics & Case-Insensitive
Text
Design simple search behavior while understanding its database trade-offs

Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

search=payroll

v

OR title/description

v

PostgreSQL text matching

Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract.

Search is not the same as exact filtering
Filtering asks for exact structured attributes such as status=IN_PROGRESS. Search usually asks whether text
resembles a user-entered phrase. TaskFlow begins with a deliberately simple case-insensitive substring search
across title and description.

...(query.search
? {
OR: [
{ title: { contains: query.search, mode: "insensitive" } },
{ description: { contains: query.search, mode: "insensitive" } },
],
}
: {})

Request                                                 Meaning

?status=DONE                                            Exact structured filter

?priority=HIGH                                          Exact structured filter

?search=payroll                                         Text contains search across chosen fields

?status=DONE&search;=payroll                            DONE tasks AND text search

Search semantics must be documented
Does search mean starts-with, contains, token matching, fuzzy matching, or full-text relevance? A production API
must choose. Phase 15 chooses contains so behavior stays obvious while the architecture is learned.

B-tree index warning

PostgreSQL substring search such as ILIKE/contains is not automatically accelerated by an ordinary B-tree index. If TaskFlow
search becomes large or latency-sensitive, measure it and consider a search-specific strategy such as trigram or full-text
indexing. Do not pretend a normal title index solves arbitrary substring search.

Search is product behavior, not a database checkbox
A payroll system might search employee code, legal name, and payroll batch number. Procurement might search PO
number, supplier, and description. The fields and semantics should reflect user tasks, then database design follows.

Safe Sorting & Stable Order
Allow-list sort fields and add deterministic tie-breaking for pagination

Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

sort + order

v

Allow-list mapping

v

Primary order

v

Unique tiebreaker

Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract.

Sorting must be allow-listed
Never accept an arbitrary field name and inject it into dynamic ordering. Phase 15 validates sort against a small public
set and maps each option to a known Prisma orderBy shape.

private buildOrderBy(sort: TaskSortField, order: SortOrder) {
switch (sort) {
case "updatedAt":
return [{ updatedAt: order }, { id: "asc" }];
case "dueAt":
return [{ dueAt: order }, { id: "asc" }];
case "title":
return [{ title: order }, { id: "asc" }];
case "createdAt":
default:
return [{ createdAt: order }, { id: "asc" }];
}
}

Why add id as a tiebreaker?
createdAt, dueAt, updatedAt, and title are not guaranteed unique. Without a deterministic secondary key, rows tied on
the primary sort can move between requests, making paginated results appear unstable.

Figure 1 - Stable ordering

Sort by createdAt desc

v

Several rows share timestamp

v

Tie remains ambiguous

v

Add id asc tiebreaker

v

One deterministic total order

Stable pagination starts with stable ordering.

Null sorting deserves a product decision
dueAt is optional. Decide whether tasks without due dates should appear first or last when sorting by dueAt.
Prisma/PostgreSQL support explicit null ordering in appropriate query shapes, but the course keeps the initial
mapping simple and asks you to make the product decision before optimizing the query.

Sorting is part of the API contract

Changing default sort later can visibly reorder every page. Treat it like behavior, not an implementation detail.

Offset Pagination & Count Metadata
Implement numbered pages with skip/take and truthful totals

Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

page/pageSize

v

skip/take

v

findMany + count

v

data + meta

Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract.

Offset pagination is the first TaskFlow implementation
Offset pagination maps naturally to numbered pages. Prisma expresses it with skip and take. The SQL concept is
OFFSET/LIMIT. This is easy to understand and fits administrative tables where users expect page numbers and direct
page navigation.

const skip = (query.page - 1) * query.pageSize;

const items = await prisma.task.findMany({
where,
orderBy,
skip,
take: query.pageSize,
});

page                   pageSize                  skip                       rows requested

1                      20                        0                          1-20

2                      20                        20                         21-40

3                      50                        100                        101-150

The deep-page trade-off
Offset pagination becomes more expensive as the offset grows because the database still has to advance past earlier
rows. That does not make offset pagination wrong; it means you should use it where numbered navigation matters
and dataset depth is reasonable, then measure real performance.

Count the same filtered set
For numbered pages, the UI often wants totalItems and totalPages. The count query must use the same where filter
as the page query. If the filters differ, the metadata lies.

const [items, totalItems] = await prisma.$transaction([
prisma.task.findMany({ where, orderBy, skip, take: pageSize }),
prisma.task.count({ where }),
]);

Why group page + count?

This groups the two related reads into one database transaction call and keeps their query intent together. It does not mean
every read-only list endpoint always requires a transaction; it is one practical way to execute related operations together in this
course.

Cursor Pagination & Strategy Selection
Understand feed-style pagination and choose it for the right product interaction

Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Product navigation need

v

Offset or cursor

v

Stable traversal

Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract.

Cursor pagination solves a different product problem
Cursor pagination resumes after a known record instead of asking the database to skip N previous rows. It is often a
better fit for feeds, infinite scroll, exports, and very deep traversal.

Requirement                                        Offset                         Cursor

Jump directly to page 42                           Excellent                      Poor fit

Infinite scroll                                    Works but can get expensive    Excellent

Human-readable page numbers                        Excellent                      Not natural

Very deep traversal                                Can degrade                    Usually stronger

Stable under frequent inserts                      Can shift                      Often more stable with correct cursor/order

Simple implementation                              Very simple                    Requires cursor strategy

// Concept-only example: cursor pagination needs a deliberately stable cursor strategy.
// TaskFlow implements offset pagination first because the current UI uses page numbers.

const page = await prisma.task.findMany({
take: 20,
cursor: cursorId ? { id: cursorId } : undefined,
skip: cursorId ? 1 : 0,
orderBy: { id: "asc" },
});

// Real production feeds often need a cursor aligned with the desired ordering.
// With random UUID ids and createdAt ordering, design the cursor intentionally
// instead of assuming offset and cursor pagination are interchangeable.

A cursor must align with ordering
Do not copy a cursor example mechanically. If the product sorts by createdAt but the cursor is unrelated to that order,
boundary behavior can become surprising. A robust feed normally uses an order and cursor strategy that together
define one stable traversal, often including a unique tiebreaker.

Figure 1 - Pagination decision

Does UI need numbered pages / direct jumps?

v

Yes -> offset is reasonable

v

No -> is traversal/feed very deep?

v

Yes -> design cursor pagination

v

Measure real behavior and workload

Choose from product interaction and dataset behavior, not from fashion.

TaskFlow choice

The current TaskFlow Tasks screen is an administrative collection, so Phase 15 implements offset pagination. Cursor
pagination remains part of your engineering toolbox for later feeds and exports.

Paginated Response Contract
Return collection data with explicit navigation metadata instead of a bare array

Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination

Architecture milestone

Response envelope

Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract.

A paginated response needs a deliberate envelope
Returning only Task[] forces the frontend to guess whether more data exists. TaskFlow adds metadata that directly
supports numbered navigation and summary text.

{
"data": [ ... ],
"meta": {
"page": 2,
"pageSize": 20,
"totalItems": 143,
"totalPages": 8,
"hasPreviousPage": true,
"hasNextPage": true
}
}

Calculate metadata centrally
const totalPages = Math.ceil(totalItems / query.pageSize);

return {
data: items,
meta: {
page: query.page,
pageSize: query.pageSize,
totalItems,
totalPages,
hasPreviousPage: query.page > 1,
hasNextPage: query.page < totalPages,
},
};

What if page is beyond the last page?
There are several defensible contracts: return an empty data array with accurate metadata, clamp to the last page, or
reject the page. TaskFlow uses the simplest explicit behavior: page remains what the client requested and data may
be empty. The metadata tells the truth. Do not silently move the client to another page unless the API documents that
policy.

Counts are not free

COUNT(*) over a heavily filtered or joined dataset can become expensive. Numbered-page UX may justify it; infinite-scroll
APIs often avoid exact totals. Product requirements and measurement determine whether totalItems belongs in the contract.

Index-Aware Query Design
Connect real query shapes to PostgreSQL indexes without over-indexing

Phase 15 - Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Observe query

v

EXPLAIN / measure

v

Candidate index

v

Measure again

Phase 15 turns an unbounded collection endpoint into a validated, queryable, stable, paginated API contract.

Indexes should follow real collection queries
Phase 10 already added indexes for project/status and assignee/status. Phase 15 teaches how to evaluate whether
listing and sorting patterns need additional support. Do not generate an index for every filter combination.

Common query shape                                             Index idea to evaluate

projectId + status                                             Existing [projectId,status]

assigneeId + status                                            Existing [assigneeId,status]

projectId + createdAt ordering                                 Possible [projectId,createdAt]

projectId + status + createdAt                                 Possible [projectId,status,createdAt] if measured

substring title/description search                             Different search-specific strategy may be needed

Multicolumn index order matters
For PostgreSQL B-tree indexes, leading columns matter most. An index on (projectId,status,createdAt) is especially
useful for queries that constrain the leading projectId and then status before ordering/scanning createdAt. It is not a
magical index for every combination of those columns.

Figure 1 - Index design loop

Observe real endpoint query

v

Inspect generated SQL / EXPLAIN

v

Measure latency and rows scanned

v

Identify repeated predicate/order pattern

v

Add minimal useful index

v

Measure again

Index design is empirical engineering, not schema decoration.

Sorting can sometimes use an index
PostgreSQL B-tree indexes can provide ordered scans. A matching index may avoid a separate sort step, but planner
choices depend on selectivity, table size, and the full query. Keep using EXPLAIN instead of guessing.

Write cost remains real

Every extra index consumes storage and must be maintained on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. A read optimization is never
free.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 15: Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
URL query state -> validated query object -> Prisma where/order/cursor -> PostgreSQL plan -> page response -> frontend navigation

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Unbounded page size
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Client sends database column names unchecked

Failure drill 4 — Counting/filtering with different predicates so metadata lies

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 15 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Implement scalable list endpoints with validated filtering/search/sorting/pagination and deterministic database queries.

Required artifact
Task list API with filter/search/sort/page contract plus metadata and indexes justified by measured query patterns.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can design a stable list contract.
• Can validate sort/filter input.
• Can explain offset vs cursor tradeoffs.
• Can connect indexes to actual query patterns.

Independent build sequence
1. Write the query contract including defaults and maximum page size.
2. Whitelist sortable fields and directions instead of interpolating arbitrary user input.
3. Implement filters and text search with clearly defined case/field semantics.
4. Start with offset pagination, then explain where cursor pagination changes consistency/performance.
5. Guarantee deterministic ordering with a unique tie-breaker.
6. Inspect representative query plans/index needs rather than indexing every field.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.
